gore or graphic violence

lots of blood just for shock value

nudity/s\*xual content

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. Return of the Living Dead will forever be the best "This ain't your Grandpa's zombies!" story.

**Score:** 176
**Body:** I swear to God, I see SO many zombie stories where they establish, "Oh yeah, these aren't Zombies, pffft, what are we, Plants? No, these are something different, something above the typical brain-eating roamers that your Little Brother is scared of, lol," and then the story just goes on like a typical zombie apocalypse story.

The first example I think of when I say this is *28 Days Later*. Great movie, I loved it, but....they establish that the zombies in this world aren't actual zombies, they're just infected with a "rage virus" but....why establish that when the Infected look and act like Zombies? Why can't they just be zombies? The movie obviously does some interesting things with them, especially with how fast and aggressive they are, but the distinction between "zombies" and "infected people" feels more important in the movie's explanation than it actually is to the story. Functionally, you're still watching people trying to survive an outbreak of monsters who were once human.

Another example I think of, which tackles the other side of the story, is *Crossed*. And I'm not talking about the Crossed here, I'm talking about the Survivors. Because they are some of the most generic Zombie Story Survivors I've ever seen; The Generic Leader, the generic Badass woman, the generic Cute Kid, the generic Best Friend, the generic Best Friend's love interest, the generic stoic guy with a dead family, the generic Asshole who gets killed off. The most interesting thing they do with these guys is making the Old Man secretly a former serial killer, and even that doesn't really go anywhere.

And I hate how the series acts like it's so DARK and EXTREME whenever it kills off a kid character, like even ignoring how they do this shit numerous times and somehow expect the audience to have the exact same reaction every time, one of the most famous scenes in *The Walking Dead* (which this series is supposed to be a corrupted version of) has a kid death! Killing a child isn't automatically some revolutionary statement about how cruel your world is. Eventually, if you keep doing it, it just becomes another part of the formula.

This is why I believe *Return* does this type of story best.

Not only are the Zombies something interesting and new while still being a clear homage to the old Romero movies, but the Survivors are something interesting and new too. They don't just feel like a collection of familiar archetypes who were assembled because every zombie story needs a Leader, a Badass, a Kid, and an Asshole. The characters actually feel like they belong to the specific world *Return* has created, rather than feeling like characters who could be dropped into literally any other zombie apocalypse story and function exactly the same.

And that's really what I think makes *Return* work so well: it understands that changing the zombies isn't enough\*\*.\*\* If you're going to establish that your undead, or undead-adjacent creatures, work differently from traditional zombies, then the world and the people living in it should feel different too. Otherwise, what's the point? You can call them "infected," "carriers," "the risen," or whatever cool name you want, but if the story is still just "a group of survivors hides in a building, someone gets bitten, the asshole betrays everyone, and then they have to escape the horde," then you've basically just put a different coat of paint on the same zombie story.

*Return* feels much more interested in asking what its particular version of the zombie apocalypse would actually DO to people and society. The zombies aren't just there to provide a different monster design; their existence affects the characters, their relationships, and the way the world operates. And because the survivors themselves have more going on than just being recognizable zombie-story archetypes, the human side of the story actually feels like part of the premise rather than filler between zombie attacks.

## 2. This movie probably has some of the worst dialogue ever written (The Happening 2008)

The plot is okay, enough to keep my attention. But I just can't stand the dialogue lol. Contrary to the consensus that the acting is bad, I do think it's the dialogue's fault.

And the background characters are absolute NPCs. What do you mean you need the main character to make decisions for you? This isn't some Telltale game.

One of the side characters literally got blown away by a shotgun for NOT having any spatial awareness whatsoever. That kid could've just taken a bit of cover, or, better yet, run, and he'd have been fine.

But overall, this was a fun movie to watch. (I don't think that's a good thing, though, because it moves pretty far away from the director's intention.) But I had a lot of fun watching it and laughing at the dialogue.

He acknowledges he can't be with his civilian wife, but Ilsa is here. The team stops a huge global-impacting disaster and kills off the Syndicate leader Solomon Lane, so that's tied off. 
4. And the constant repetition of things like: Everything has been building up to this Ethan! This is what you are meant to do Ethan! You could make a drinking game out of it.
5. To be fair, each act in the movie is better than the one before it. 1st act is very clunky, exposition heavy to an unnecessary degree and overdone on the Ethan worship.

2nd act is better. Still a bit of all those problems, but a great double fight scene set piece and an incredible underwater sequence.

3rd act features an incredible airborne sequence which is an incredible finish for the mission.

But yeah those first 30-40 min are pretty damn rough.
  - As a huge fan of the franchise, the entire movie was badly written and the climax was very disappointing. The previous three (4,5,6) were less dialogue and exposition heavy, moved between action scenes more smoothly and were a more tight experience overall. Fallout is one of the best action movies ever in my opinion. 

Final reckoning has 3-4 amazing scenes and what’s in between is just a slog to get through.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I hate peoples obsession with realism

**Score:** 56
**Body:** Like I understand it as genre of its own, if there are like 20 categories…it can be one.

But people complain about it…be it superhero films or over the top action or just stylish drama.

Nolan ruined it with Batman, everyone was trying to recreate grounded superhero genre,it took years to embrace the campiness again.

When I used to watch movies, best thing used to be how stylish it is. Like be it fashion, or beautiful women or unrealistic but impactful dialogues.

Think of the gentlemen, Peaky blinders, upcoming Street Fighter.

9 out of 10 film should be allowed to embrace its campiness. Most usually gain from style.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I recall the director of *If I Had Legs I’d Kick You*, Mary Bronstein, mentioned in a Q&A that she felt similarly—and that her approach to the movie was to let the tone guide the film rather than be grounded by realism. I wish more films would take that approach.
2. I think there is a difference between something seeming plausible and realism. Batman is something that seems plausible and isn’t realism. So, I think you’re conflating what realism means to fit your opinion. But that’s just my opinion.
3. Thank you. One of my biggest pet peeves about online movie discussions is when people situate the FICTION their watching into reality. It’s like they’re watching reality tv than a F MOVIE. Sorry, it just peeves me like no other 
4. So by "realism" you mean the "grounded" and "formalist" approach to adapting something which is normally fantasical? Your not talking about like Italian Postwar Realism or Iranian Realism? Words have meaning and I think "Realism" already has a particular meaning in film criticism. 

Anyway, yah I agree that studios were chasing that dragon for a long time. But why are we still complaing about it? Even Superhero movies have moved away from that, James Gunn loves comic bookyness for the DC stuff and Fantasic Four is the most expressionistic Marvel film yet.
5. I worked on a film once that ended up being a very moving, well-crafted costume melodrama in my opinion, but it got hit with negative reviews from tons of critics who dinged it for being “melodramatic.” I just remember being like “yes that’s the genre? What else is wrong with it?” How is that a legitimate critique? I always respected Ebert for being open about when a movie wasn’t the style or drama he liked but he still appreciated the execution.
6. It's all about the tone the movie establishes. I watched *Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass* the other night. That movie very quickly establishes that it is a heightened universe, and strange events and behaviors are to be expected. However, if a movie doesn't manage the tone, starts serious and then has a moment of unexplained absurdity, it can be jarring.
7. If the film can establish that it wont be grounded in realism in the first 10 minutes, most of the time the audience can go along for the ride.

Yorgos Lanthimos is a good example of this
8. Batman isn’t very realistic at all though. It’s grounded, but the actual world and what Batman does in it are still pretty insane. The fact that it feels realistic is Nolan’s filmmaking doing its job and selling you the illusion. The copy cats never understood that. But.. yes. more or less what Paperweight22 said above
9. It’s worth understanding why realism is important to people.

People come to movies for many different reasons, but they are always coming from the real world and taking stuff from the real world in with them. When they leave, they are  leaving to the real world and hopefully taking stuff with them there.

Comparison to the real world is unavoidable, in that comparison is where you do your work to dazzle, entertain, teach…

When you diverge from the real world you’re asking the audience to make an allowance in order for you to show them something.

Realism is effective and popular because (I think) it gives the audience less work to do to engage with what they’re being shown. Any differences you do add though become a contrast in the audiences mind, they stick out. If that isn’t part of what you’re trying to show them, it looks like a mistake, and that’s where you get criticism and the obsession with realism.

## 2. 12 MONKEYS Mesmerized And Perplexed Me Like Never Before.

**Score:** 26
**Body:** First of all. I would say that I **Absolutely** loved the movie. It was an unforgettable experience. I didn't expect it to be this much fun. The whole movie was a fever dream, felt like a surgical theatre. Clinical, sterile, grainy, blurry. I enjoyed every second of it, every single performance there.

And that ending was so bleak, hopeless and depressing. Considering the tone of the rest of the movie, I expected a win, some catharsis. It doesn't offer one. Felt like a prick, really.

Terry Gilliam blended and balanced serious and broad themes of time travel, psychology, post apocalyptic future, consumerism, control, potential future warfare, the plight of humanity brought on by humanity itself, all in 120 minutes or so. Though I haven't seen Brazil, I've researched about it, and I can see this movie has strong shades of it.

I found it visually spectacular. The post-apocalyptic world is built exactly to induce sheer uncanniness, the costumes, the machines. And the contemporary past is built as the complete opposite, a dream, something beautiful, something not to let go of, something to cherish. I also loved how dystopia isn't the main focus. It's shown subtly, yet effectively enough that I had no issue filling in the gaps myself. The movie mostly stays with the present timeline, and that's the beauty of it.

Terry Gilliam is a genius in feeding the audience the right way, mostly. Take the time travel sequences for example. Cole travels to the present three times, but the time machine and its exact mechanics are only shown once, on the second trip. That removed redundancy and kept the substance alive over style.

But the script fell flat for me right in the end. I can guess that Cole was dreaming of his own death as a kid, which is straight from La Jetée, (the original short this whole film is expanding on) and that part I don't mind, it's earned, seeded right from the opening frame. My issue is everything Gilliam built around it.

Compare this to Dark City, a film I also had gaps with, but there, act one tells you outright that the world might not be real, so every unanswered question afterward still sits inside a world you were told to distrust. 12 Monkeys never does that. The 90s scenes play completely straight, sane, grounded, no cue anywhere telling you to question them the way Dark City does from minute one. So when the ending suddenly refuses to answer basic questions, it doesn't feel like trust in the audience, it feels like a debt never paid. Now I don't mean that there should have been a narration, voice over or an explanation, but that twist happened too jarringly, just wanted that "Ah, there it is" moment.

And there's more. Who was the voice in Cole's head? Why did he call him Bob? Why did he have a similar voice to that homeless toothless man? Speaking of teeth, why did Cole remove his teeth? Who was watching him? Which reality is the real one? Was the virus even really spread, and if it was, what did the scientists actually gain by sending Cole back to die? Is the dystopia the dream, or is the 90s the dream? Who was the kid, really?

Right at the start, Cole's in a hazmat suit collecting a specimen from the exact spot he gets shot in '96, was that real, staged, or programmed? Was Jeffrey right that they studied his mind and built an alternate world out of it? Why did Jose tell Cole to "kill the lady?"

Most importantly, for most of the runtime, Cole is a pawn, a tool being moved around for a cause bigger than him. Then suddenly, in the last stretch, the movie wants this to be personal, his own psychological tragedy, his own dream, his own loop, without ever doing the legwork earlier to make that the actual throughline. The shift isn't earned, it's just handed to you in the last ten minutes.

Now I'm speculating about some things. I guess that maybe everything is a construct of Cole's own thoughts. Or maybe Cole was chosen only because his dream about his own death was more vivid than others. But I should say that this movie really had made it hard for me to guess or speculate about its aspects, harder than many movies I have watched. And none of these are the flaws of the movie, I just want to put everything together.

What do you think of it? Would love to hear from you.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I always thought that Cole's dreams of the ending at the airport were actually memories. That the boy at the airport was young Cole watching his future self die.

My favourite scene is the cinema when they watch Vertigo. Cole is musing about only noticing scenes in a film the second time you watch it. I only really noticed Cole's dialogue in this scene on rewatch because there's so much plot focused stuff drawing your attention. Great meta long game by Gilliam.

The film is kind of an inverse Vertigo. Instead of a traveller from the past that turns out to be fake you have a traveller from the future who turns out to be genuine.
2. None of it was a dream.  It was a time travel loop.  They got things wrong about the details of the past. It’s implied at the end there were other agents sent after Cole’s death, based on what they learned from Cole.

The tragedy of Cole is he witnessed his own death as a child.
3. One of my all time favorites. Brad Pitt’s best role imo and the acting across the board is great.

When Bruce Willis hears Blueberry Hill my heart wants to break and of all the depictions of future dystopias, one that depicts a world without music is personally a deeply terrifying prospect.

It also does a pretty great job at keeping the audience guessing. And the end. I generally hate endings without resolutions but this one was exceptional. Was the doctor/scientist on the plane there on her first trip through that timeline or was she sent back? Both are equally plausible but have very different implications.

I just leaned it’s based on a French film ~~Le Jette~~ La Jetée so I gotta watch that in the near future.

Edit: corrected the French film’s title
  - That moment when he breaks down in the car broke me too. An adult man crying to a music piece is hard to see really. Kinda reminded me of Equilibrium where Christian Bale cries while listening to music. Bruce Willis's character got so vulnerable and naive, suddenly changing the course of the whole movie. It's not a frequently discussed film, but when it is, the narrative is that it's the Heaven's Gate of the Japanese New Wave. A ridiculously overlong location shoot (18 months!) that arguably ended Nikkatsu's golden age and inarguably derailed Imamura's career for over a decade. 

It's a weird, atmospheric, haunting film about the collision between the "primitive" and the modern. It's also a lengthy, languid portrait of Okinawa, with frequent cuts to various wildlife that some critics have compared to the films of Terence Malick. 

Honestly, I'm not sure how I feel about the film. It's a big, sprawling, weird thing that's clearly the product of an auteur vision. At the same time, I'm not sure it really comes together into a great film. But it does have some really incredible, striking moments that will stay with me.

## 4. Is it a moral failure if a filmmaker tries to communicate a cultural idea without fully fleshing out the characters that represent that culture?

**Score:** 9
**Body:** That title may be confusing so I will elaborate.

I see a fair amount of outrage towards films that try to communicate certain ideas about race, gender, sexual orientation, class, etc. When the characters in the film that embody those demographics are more of an idea than a fully fleshed out character.

I'm finding myself a bit torn on this, because on one hand it is always better to have well realized representations of all types of people in a film. On the other hand, if the idea is still effectively communicated, I consider it a net positive. I think you can still empathize with a real type of person through an archetypal rendering.

I'm thinking of this with James Gray's Armageddon Time in mind. I thought the film was fantastic and gave it 5 stars on Letterboxd. I felt very deeply for the character of Johnny, a black boy that the Jewish protagonist (Paul) befriends while the two misbehave in school. The film may not fully explore the inner world of Johnny, and instead focuses on his position in the Paul's world and the micro and macro aggressions Paul witnesses him face. Ultimately the arc of their relationship is about privilege, the disparity of consequences the two face, Paul's failure to advocate for Johnny, and the unease in moving forward in complicity.

The film isn't a perfect, didactic, tidy lesson in race and privilege. It's a personal exploration and I mostly took it at face value. It's also not the \*only\* subject matter in the film.

But I'm seeing a lot of people basically outraged at the film's failure to add enough nuance and depth to the character of Johnny and that seems to undermine everything else the film is going for. I know online reviews can be bottom of the barrel but it has me questioning things.
